meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to a point where he does not discern any truth'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Dostoevsky, from The Brothers Karamazov. The familiar English wording is Pevear & Volokhonsky's 1990 translation, and the line is usually cut short.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine Dostoevsky. The line is spoken by the elder Zosima to Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov in The Brothers Karamazov, Part One, Book II, chapter 2 (“The Old Buffoon”) — the novel Dostoevsky serialised in The Russian Messenger from January 1879 to November 1880. This exact English wording, though, is not Dostoevsky’s: it is the 1990 translation by Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky, and the sentence is almost always cut off mid–clause.

source.excerpt: The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others.
trail: Located the passage in the novel itself: the full Constance Garnett translation at Project Gutenberg ↗ carries it in Book II, “An Unfortunate Gathering,” chapter II, “The Old Buffoon,” spoken by Father Zossima to Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov.

Matched the popular wording to its translator: Wikiquote’s sourced Dostoyevsky page ↗ prints this exact sentence and credits it to the translation by Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky (1990), p. 44.

Dated the translation: Wikipedia’s account of Pevear and Volokhonsky ↗ records that their Brothers Karamazov was accepted by North Point Press, a small San Francisco house, and went on to win a PEN/Book-of-the-Month Club Translation Prize.
Confirmed the novel’s own dates: Wikipedia’s article on the novel ↗ states it was published as a serial in The Russian Messenger from January 1879 to November 1880, with the separate edition in 1880.
source.excerptNote: That is Constance Garnett’s wording, from the public-domain text at Project Gutenberg ↗. The version that circulates online — “comes to a point where he does not discern any truth” — is the later Pevear and Volokhonsky rendering, whose full sentence continues “…either in himself or anywhere around him, and thus falls into disrespect towards himself and others.”

Dostoevsky’s Russian original (serialised 1879–1880) is long in the public domain, as is Constance Garnett’s English translation, which Project Gutenberg distributes freely ↗. author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.heading: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.bio: Fyodor Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, short-story writer, essayist and journalist, widely regarded as one of the greatest novelists in world literature. His late fiction — Crime and Punishment, Demons, The Brothers Karamazov — is preoccupied with exactly the problem Zosima names here: what happens to a person who can no longer tell the truth from his own account of it. He died on 9 February 1881, months after finishing the serialisation of The Brothers Karamazov.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fake — it is a real sentence from a real novel. What gets mangled is everything around it: who is speaking, who wrote the English, and where the sentence is supposed to stop.

items.who: Father Zosima, not Dostoevsky in his own voice
items.why: The line is dialogue. In the text at Project Gutenberg ↗ it is the elder Zossima speaking to Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, who has just asked what he must do to gain eternal life. Dostoevsky wrote it; a monk in his novel says it. Both facts are true and quote cards keep only the first.

“Comes to a point where he does not discern any truth” is their 1990 rendering, credited as such on Wikiquote ↗. Garnett has “comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth”; other editions differ again. A Goodreads search ↗ returns several of these variants side by side, all filed simply under “Fyodor Dostoevsky” with no translator named.

The quotation as it travels stops at “does not discern any truth.” Wikiquote’s full text ↗ shows the clause running on — “either in himself or anywhere around him, and thus falls into disrespect towards himself and others” — and then to the point Zosima is actually building toward, about a self-deceiver being the first to take offence.

misattribution.truthLine: Dostoevsky wrote the thought and put it in Zosima’s mouth; Pevear and Volokhonsky wrote the English you have read. Cite The Brothers Karamazov ↗ — and name the translator.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The scene is almost comic before it turns serious. Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov — a buffoon, a drunk, a man who performs his own shamelessness — kneels before the revered elder Zosima and asks, more or less as a stunt, what he must do to gain eternal life. Zosima does not play along. He answers the question as though it were sincere, and tells him to stop lying to himself.

That is the move that gives the line its force. It is not general wisdom offered from a lectern; it is aimed at one specific man who has built a personality out of self-deception, and who is at that moment deceiving himself about why he is kneeling. Dostoevsky then lets Zosima follow the logic all the way down: lose the ability to tell truth from falsehood, and you lose self-respect; lose self-respect, and you stop being able to love.
detailsBody: The passage sits in Part One, Book II of the novel, the long gathering at the monastery where the Karamazov family assembles and immediately disgraces itself. Dostoevsky uses the setting to put his most disciplined character in a room with his least disciplined one.
The Brothers Karamazov was the last novel Dostoevsky completed. Its serialisation in The Russian Messenger ended in November 1880, and he died on 9 February 1881.

sourcesVerified.claim: The Brothers Karamazov contains the passage "The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others," spoken by Father Zossima to Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, in Book II ("An Unfortunate Gathering"), chapter II, "The Old Buffoon"; translation by Constance Garnett.

Wikiquote's sourced Dostoyevsky page reproduces the exact wording "A man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to a point where he does not discern any truth either in himself or anywhere around him, and thus falls into disrespect towards himself and others" and attributes it to the translation by Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky (1990), p. 44. It also carries the continuation "A man who lies to himself is often the first to take offense."

The Brothers Karamazov was published as a serial in The Russian Messenger from January 1879 to November 1880, with a separate edition in 1880; the English translations list includes Richard Pevear and Larissa Volokhonsky (1990).

Pevear and Volokhonsky's Brothers Karamazov translation was accepted by North Point Press, a small publishing house in San Francisco, and went on to win a PEN/Book-of-the-Month Club Translation Prize.

Fyodor Dostoevsky was born 11 November 1821 and died 9 February 1881; he was a Russian novelist, short-story writer, essayist and journalist regarded as one of the greatest novelists in world literature.

Multiple competing English translations of this passage circulate attributed simply to "Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov" with no translator credited — including both the Garnett-style "cannot distinguish the truth within him" wording and the Pevear/Volokhonsky "does not discern any truth" wording.
